slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself concretely in writing: if a Josephson junction were replaced with an ordinary linear inductor, explain specifically what would go wrong when applying a microwave pulse meant to flip the qubit from |0> to |1>, naming the evenly-spaced-ladder problem and why the pulse would also drive the 1-to-2 transition. Then draw (as a labeled diagram or sketch description) the basic LC-oscillator-plus-Josephson-junction circuit and mark where the nonlinearity lives.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of the leakage/addressability failure that occurs without a Josephson junction, plus a labeled circuit sketch showing the nonlinear element's location.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself with a written tradeoff analysis: if an engineer increased a transmon's shunting capacitance further to reduce charge-noise sensitivity even more, explain what happens to anharmonicity and what new design problem that creates for microwave control pulses. Then write a short comparison table (charge qubit vs. transmon) naming the noise sensitivity and anharmonicity tradeoff each makes.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of the capacitance-vs-anharmonicity tradeoff from the Check Yourself scenario, plus a two-row comparison table contrasting charge qubits and transmons on noise sensitivity and anharmonicity.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself with real arithmetic: for a qubit with T1=150 microseconds and measured T2=90 microseconds, use 1/T2 = 1/(2*T1) + 1/T-phi to solve for T-phi, confirm the result is physically plausible (T2 less than 2*T1), and state what it implies about T-phi relative to T1. Show your algebra.
slots.deliverable: Your worked algebra solving for T-phi given T1=150us and T2=90us, with a written statement of whether the result is physically plausible and what it implies about the relative size of T-phi versus T1.

lessons.title: Dilution Refrigerators & Why Qubits Need Them

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: if an engineering team scaled a superconducting processor from a few dozen qubits to many thousands using one dedicated physical control line per qubit all the way into the mixing chamber, name the two specific physical constraints inside the dilution refrigerator they'd run into first (finite wiring space, finite cooling power at the coldest stage) and explain why each one bites.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation naming the two specific physical constraints (wiring/feedthrough space and cooling-power budget) that block naive per-qubit wiring at scale, with reasoning for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself as a written rebuttal: a news article claims 'Company A's new chip has more qubits than Company B's, so it is strictly the more capable quantum computer.' Using coherence time, gate fidelity, and connectivity from this lesson, explain specifically why that conclusion doesn't follow. Then write one sentence each summarizing IBM's, Google's, and Rigetti's distinct strategic emphasis.
slots.deliverable: A written rebuttal of the qubit-count-only claim citing coherence time, fidelity, and connectivity, plus three one-sentence summaries of IBM's, Google's, and Rigetti's respective strategic bets.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: explain what's actually being traded when a trapped-ion qubit avoids on-chip fabrication but still requires a vacuum chamber, lasers, and precise electrode voltages just to exist as a qubit at all. Then write a short paragraph contrasting this with the superconducting qubit's fabrication-plus-cryostat requirement from Chapter 1, naming which specific engineering burden each platform avoids and which it still carries.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of what trapped-ion hardware trades away versus what it still requires, plus a short comparison paragraph against the superconducting platform's own tradeoffs.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: explain why a trapped-ion two-qubit gate can't work by simply shining a laser at both ions simultaneously the way a single-qubit gate addresses one ion, and name the additional physical mechanism (the chain's shared motional mode / phonon bus) that has to be involved and why. Then compute, using the lesson's illustrative numbers (roughly 50ns superconducting vs roughly 20 microseconds trapped-ion), the approximate speed ratio between the two gate types.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of why shared motional modes, not simultaneous laser addressing, are required for trapped-ion two-qubit gates, plus your computed speed ratio between the two illustrative gate times.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: a trapped-ion vendor advertises 'full connectivity' for its processor. Using what you now know about motional mode crowding, write the specific qualification you'd add to that claim, and explain why it matters for how the system actually scales to larger qubit counts (i.e. why it eventually needs shuttling or photonic interconnects between smaller chains rather than one ever-longer chain).
slots.deliverable: A written qualification of the 'full connectivity' marketing claim naming motional-mode-crowding as the real limit, plus an explanation of why scaling requires shuttling or photonic links instead of simply lengthening the chain.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: a press release says a trapped-ion system has 'industry-leading two-qubit gate fidelity.' Name the two pieces of missing context you'd want before treating that as meaningful (which system generation/benchmark methodology, and whether it holds across a full connected array, not just an isolated pair), and explain why the QCCD architecture matters specifically for interpreting qubit-count claims from these vendors.
slots.deliverable: A written list of the two missing context pieces needed to evaluate the fidelity press release, plus an explanation of why QCCD architecture complicates a simple qubit-count comparison.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: a friend claims trapped-ion computers are 'strictly better' than superconducting computers because their two-qubit gates have higher reported fidelity. Using at least two other dimensions from this lesson (gate speed, scaling bottleneck type, cost/footprint), write a rebuttal explaining why that conclusion doesn't follow. Build a four-row comparison table (speed, connectivity, fidelity, scaling bottleneck) for the two platforms as you write it.
slots.deliverable: A written rebuttal of the 'strictly better' claim citing at least two additional dimensions, plus your own four-row superconducting-vs-trapped-ion comparison table.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: a colleague says 'photonic qubits don't decohere the way superconducting qubits do, so photonic computers should have an easier error problem.' Explain what's missing from that claim and name the real dominant error source in photonic systems instead (photon loss, which has no error-correction analog since the physical carrier simply ceases to exist). Write one paragraph contrasting photon loss against T1/T2 decoherence from Chapter 1.
slots.deliverable: A written correction of the colleague's claim naming photon loss as the real dominant error source, plus a paragraph contrasting it against T1/T2-style decoherence.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: PsiQuantum and Xanadu are both 'photonic quantum computing companies,' but their near-term strategies look very different. Write a clear explanation of the core difference in what each company is optimizing for right now (PsiQuantum: silicon-photonics manufacturing scale toward a long-horizon fault-tolerant machine; Xanadu: continuous-variable cloud-accessible hardware today via Gaussian boson sampling).
slots.deliverable: A written explanation distinguishing PsiQuantum's manufacturing-scale fault-tolerant bet from Xanadu's near-term continuous-variable cloud strategy, naming each company's specific technical approach.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: explain in your own words why individually steerable optical tweezers (rather than fixed physical traps) give neutral-atom hardware a kind of flexibility fabricated-trap platforms don't have. Then write a short explanation of the Rydberg blockade mechanism, naming specifically what happens to a second nearby atom when one atom is already excited to a Rydberg state, and why that's useful for building a two-qubit gate.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of why movable tweezers give reconfigurability that fabricated traps lack, plus a written explanation of the Rydberg blockade mechanism and its role in entangling gates.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: a news article claims 'Company X's neutral-atom computer now has the most qubits of any quantum computer in the world.' Write the specific question you should ask before treating that as evidence the system is close to outperforming other platforms on real computations (what are its gate fidelities and atom-loss rates, and are these raw trapped atoms or usable logical qubits). Name QuEra and Pasqal and one sentence on each company's analog-vs-digital positioning.
slots.deliverable: A written follow-up question exposing the raw-atom-count-vs-usable-qubit distinction, plus one sentence each on QuEra's and Pasqal's analog/digital positioning.

slots.practicalActivity: Build your own four-row comparison table (superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic, neutral-atom) across temperature, native connectivity, typical gate speed, typical fidelity regime, and biggest open scaling bottleneck, filling it in from memory using everything learned across this chapter and the two before it, then check it against the lesson's own table. Answer the Check Yourself: explain why 'which modality is the best' doesn't have a single honest answer today, and write a better version of the question.
slots.deliverable: Your own completed five-column, four-row comparison table built from memory and checked against the lesson, plus a written reframing of 'which is best' into a more honest, workload-specific question.

slots.practicalActivity: Draw (on paper or in a simple diagram) a small heavy-hex connectivity graph and a small square-grid connectivity graph, each with at least 7 nodes, labeling the edges. Then answer the lesson's Check Yourself: explain why IBM uses the sparser heavy-hex layout instead of a denser grid, naming the frequency-collision tradeoff specifically.
slots.deliverable: Your two hand-drawn connectivity graphs (heavy-hex and grid, 7+ nodes each) with edges labeled, plus a written explanation of the frequency-collision tradeoff that justifies heavy-hex over grid.

lessons.title: Why Connectivity Limits Affect Circuit Design

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's worked example by hand: for two qubits at graph distance 3 needing 2 SWAPs (6 CNOTs) plus 1 real CNOT = 7 total two-qubit operations, compute the probability of at least one error using a 0.5% per-gate error rate via 1-(1-0.005)^7, confirming the lesson's ~3.4% figure. Then answer the Check Yourself: what question about the device would you ask a circuit designer who claims their 40-two-qubit-gate algorithm 'should fit easily' within the error budget, without yet knowing connectivity.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed error probability (confirming ~3.4%) for the 7-operation routed circuit, plus a written follow-up question you'd ask the circuit designer about device connectivity before accepting their claim.

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's 40-gate-plus-20-SWAP worked example by hand: compute 20 SWAPs x 3 CNOTs = 60 extra two-qubit operations, for 100 total, then compute the error probability at a 0.5% per-gate rate using 1-(1-0.005)^40 for the native-only case and 1-(1-0.005)^100 for the routed case, confirming the lesson's roughly 18% and 39% figures. Answer the Check Yourself: why is a 5-SWAP compilation the far better choice over a 25-SWAP one even though both circuits are logically correct.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed error probabilities for the 40-gate (~18%) and 100-gate (~39%) cases, plus a written explanation of why fewer inserted SWAPs is the better real-world choice despite both circuits being logically correct.

lessons.title: Topology Lab: Reading a Real Device Map

slots.practicalActivity: If you have access, open IBM Quantum's public device map for a real backend and identify, from the live calibration overlay, a sweet-spot cluster of qubits with the lowest two-qubit edge errors versus a weaker region (screenshot or note the qubit indices and error values). If no access is available, work through the lesson's Check Yourself scenario in writing instead: Region A has native connectivity but middling error rates, Region B has excellent error rates but needs 2 extra SWAPs -- decide between them and state what you'd check before deciding.
slots.deliverable: Either a screenshot/notes identifying a real sweet-spot region versus a weaker region on an actual device map, or a written decision between Region A and Region B from the Check Yourself scenario with your reasoning and what you'd verify first.

slots.practicalActivity: Draw a labeled signal-path diagram from a room-temperature AWG through upconversion, DACs, cryostat attenuators and filters, down to the qubit chip, and back up through the HEMT/parametric amplifier chain to an ADC -- naming each component's job from the lesson. Then answer the Check Yourself: a vendor announces a 1,000-qubit chip; write the specific question about control electronics and cryostat wiring you'd ask before assuming the system is usable at that scale.
slots.deliverable: Your labeled round-trip signal-path diagram (AWG to qubit and back) naming every component's function, plus a written follow-up question challenging the 1,000-qubit announcement on wiring/control grounds.

slots.practicalActivity: Write out, in your own words, how a DRAG pulse corrects for leakage into a higher energy level compared to a naively-shaped pulse, naming the specific derivative-based correction term conceptually. Then answer the Check Yourself: why might a research team hand-tune the underlying pulse for a specific gate rather than accepting the provider's default, and what do they risk by doing so (fragility, being wrong in ways a named gate usually isn't).
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of how a DRAG pulse suppresses leakage relative to a naive pulse, plus a written answer on the benefit and the specific risk of hand-tuning pulses instead of using provider defaults.

slots.practicalActivity: List the three physical sources of qubit drift from the lesson (thermal fluctuations, TLS material defects, flux noise) with one sentence each on the mechanism. Then answer the Check Yourself: a team submits a sensitive circuit at 2 PM relying on a 6 AM calibration report -- name what could go wrong and what you'd recommend they check before trusting the result (e.g. pulling fresher calibration data, checking how fast that platform typically drifts).
slots.deliverable: Your three-item list of drift sources with mechanism explanations, plus a written recommendation for what the 2 PM team should check before trusting results from a stale 6 AM calibration.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's four-step practical workflow (identify needed connectivity, scan edge error rates, check T1/T2 against circuit runtime, check readout error on measured qubits), walk through it for an invented 5-qubit chain circuit of your own design on a hypothetical chip, writing out which qubits/edges you'd pick and why. Then answer the Check Yourself: two backends report similar median two-qubit error rates but your circuit needs a specific 5-qubit chain -- name the additional calibration data you'd check and why the median alone isn't enough.
slots.deliverable: Your worked four-step qubit-selection walkthrough for an invented 5-qubit circuit, plus a written answer naming the additional per-edge data you'd need beyond the median error rate to choose between two backends.

lessons.title: Metrics That Actually Matter: Qubit Count, Fidelity, Connectivity

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself precisely: a vendor announces a 500-qubit chip and says nothing about two-qubit gate fidelity or connectivity graph. Using the three-way AND rule (enough qubits AND enough coherent depth AND enough connectivity), explain why you can't yet conclude anything about what circuits this chip can run, and name the two specific follow-up numbers you'd ask for.
slots.deliverable: A written application of the three-way AND rule to the 500-qubit announcement, explicitly naming the two missing numbers (two-qubit gate fidelity and the connectivity graph) you'd request before judging it.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself with real computation: Device A reports QV=128, Device B reports QV=64. Using QV=2^n, solve for n on each device (n=7 and n=6 respectively) and explain what that implies about the largest square circuit each can reliably run. Then list two pieces of information this QV comparison still leaves out (e.g. execution speed/CLOPS, whether the circuit shape resembles your real workload) before choosing between them for a real project.
slots.deliverable: Your worked solution for n on both devices from QV=2^n, plus a written list of two specific pieces of missing information the QV comparison doesn't capture.

lessons.title: Choosing Hardware for a Given Workload

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself fully: a research team needs a 12-qubit chemistry simulation that's quite deep and needs several non-adjacent qubit pairs to interact directly. Using the four workload shapes from this lesson, walk through which platform type you'd recommend, what tradeoff you're accepting, and name one non-technical factor (cloud access, queue time, SDK maturity, or vendor roadmap) that could still change your answer.
slots.deliverable: A written platform recommendation for the 12-qubit deep-circuit chemistry workload, naming the specific workload shape it matches, the tradeoff accepted, and one non-technical factor that could flip the decision.

slots.practicalActivity: Complete the lesson's own Check Yourself as your capstone deliverable: using the five-section brief structure (requirements summary, candidate platforms considered, deciding tradeoff, chosen platform with honest caveats, what would change the recommendation), draft a full hardware-selection brief for a deep 4-qubit quantum simulation circuit (~40 sequential two-qubit gate layers) requiring very high per-gate fidelity, essentially no SWAP tolerance, no hard budget constraint, and a six-month research timeline.
slots.deliverable: Your complete five-section hardware-selection brief for the deep 4-qubit, 40-layer, high-fidelity workload, with every section filled in: requirements, candidates, deciding tradeoff, recommendation with caveats, and the specific condition that would change it.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student understands the real physics and engineering tradeoffs of all four major qubit modalities (superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic, neutral-atom), can read a real device's connectivity graph and calibration report to pick qubits for a circuit, can interpret composite benchmarks like Quantum Volume critically instead of trusting a headline qubit count, and has written a complete, defensible hardware-selection brief matching a real workload's requirements to a specific platform's tradeoffs.
